newsitem.title: UK: UK Labour lead will dip but win in sight -pollster.
newsitem.headline: UK Labour lead will dip but win in sight -pollster.

text.p: The Labour Party's large opinion poll lead will fall dramatically as soon as Prime Minister John Major calls the election, but the opposition is still set for a solid victory, one of Britain's top pollsters said on Wednesday.

Bob Worcester, chairman of the polling organisation MORI, said support for the ruling Conservatives would rise as soon as voters realise that Labour's current poll lead of nearly 20 points translated into a theoretical 250 seat majority.
But even after this, Labour should still win the election with a majority of 41 seats, Worcester said.
Worcester said the British public was reluctant to give any party the size of parliamentary majority implied by Labour's current 20-point poll lead.

"The British public are going to react like a mongoose to a cobra," said Worcester, adding that tactical voting would reappear, and he believed that the Liberal Democrats would do far better than suggested by many other pollsters.
But Labour's victory appeared secure. "The electorate wants a change. You can feel it, you can reach out and touch it," Worcester told reporters at a parliamentary lunch.
Worcester said polls showed that Labour's core supporters were far less likely to switch to another party than the Conservative party's core supporters.

Labour leader Tony Blair was seen by voters as a capable leader with lots of personality who was interested in Britain's problems while Major was seen as an out-of-touch, inflexible and narrow-minded politician who talked down to voters.
As a result, even a serious personal scandal involving Blair would probably still leave the main opposition party four points clear of the ruling Conservatives, he said.

Worcester traced Major's decline to Black Wednesday, the day in September 1992 when sterling crashed out of the European Exchange Rate Mechanism, dealing a body blow to the government's claim to be the surest hands at the economic tiller.
"The trauma is still there even if they've forgotten the wound," said Worcester.

The pollster also dismissed claims by right-wing Conservatives opposed to European integration that Europe is a key issue in the minds of voters, saying only 19 percent of voters believed Europe was a key factor and these were almost evenly split between Conservative and Labour supporters.

Worcester also dismissed suggestions that the minority Liberal Democrats were likely to be squeezed out between Labour and the Conservatives in the election campaign, which Major must call for May at the latest.
The Liberal Democrats were still likely to win 30 or more seats. But he added: "The Liberal Democrats are basically a protest party, a dustbin party." -- London Newsroom +44-171-542-7768
